title: How a construction company works
source: docs/learning/src/00-big-picture.html (Field Guide 00, draft 7 Nov 2026): typical figures, to be checked by someone who has run sites

scenes.title: How a construction company works
beats: Before we pitch anything, we need to understand the people we're selling to.
This is a construction company. It turns money, material and labour into a building, usually for someone else.
In the next few minutes, you'll see how it wins work, spends money, gets paid, and where its profit quietly disappears.

scenes.title: Four kinds you'll meet
beats: There are four kinds of construction company you'll meet.
Building contractors build for a client, under a contract. They are our main buyer: several sites at once, and five to fifty engineers.
Builders and developers buy land, build flats or villas, and sell them. They are their own client.
Government contractors build roads and public buildings, with tenders and strict paperwork. They come later for us.
And specialists, like electrical or plumbing firms, are often our customers' own subcontractors and suppliers.

cards.title: Building contractor
cards.text: Builds for a client under a contract. Several sites, 5 to 50 engineers.

cards.title: Builder / developer
cards.text: Buys land, builds flats or villas, sells them. Its own client.

cards.title: Government contractor
cards.text: Roads and public buildings. Tenders, strict billing rules.

scenes.title: The contract decides who carries the risk
beats: How a contractor is paid decides who carries the risk if the job costs more than planned.
With an item-rate contract, built on the BOQ, the bill of quantities, they're paid a rate for each unit of work, on the quantity actually measured.
With a lump sum, it's one fixed price for the whole job, so almost all the risk sits with the contractor.
Labour-only means the client buys the material, and the contractor supplies the people.
And cost-plus means actual cost plus a fee. The client carries the risk, but the contractor has to prove every single cost.

scenes.title: Out of every ₹100 of contract value
scenes.note: Rough ranges for building work; every company and project differs.
beats: Now, follow the money. Out of every hundred rupees a client pays...
material takes around forty to sixty.
Labour takes twenty to thirty.
Subcontractors, equipment, transport and overheads take most of the rest.
And what's left, the margin, is often only around ten rupees.
So here's the number to remember. With a ten percent margin, if just three percent of the material is lost, about a quarter of the profit is gone.

callout.small: ≈ a quarter of the profit gone

scenes.title: Six phases, from winning the job to the last rupee
beats: Every project goes through six phases.
One: win. The drawings become a BOQ, every work item with its quantity and rate. Set a rate too low, and the job loses money before the first brick.
Two: set up. The estimate becomes the budget, and the team, suppliers and subcontractors are lined up.
Three: execute. This lasts months, sometimes years. It's where most of the money is spent, and where most of it leaks.
Four: bill and collect. Every month, the work done is measured and billed to the client, as a running-account bill, an R A bill.
Five: hand over. Snags are fixed, and the final bill goes in.
And six: the defects period. Often about a year, while part of every bill, called retention, is still held back.

scenes.title: The people, and what keeps them awake
beats: Now, the people. Each one owns a piece of the business, and each one worries about something different.
The owner asks: are we making money on this project, and will the client pay on time?
The general manager releases the payments, and asks: was fifteen thousand rupees of work really done, for the fifteen thousand we paid?
The project manager watches time and cost across the sites. The site engineer runs one site, day by day.
The supervisor runs the workers. The storekeeper counts material in and out.
The quantity surveyor measures the work and checks the bills. Purchase buys. Accounts pays and collects, and an outside accountant, the C A, keeps the books in Tally.
In a small company, one person wears several of these hats. But the jobs still exist.

scenes.title: Every day, every week, every month
beats: The whole business runs to a rhythm.
Every day: work done, attendance, deliveries, material used, problems on site, photos, and the daily progress report, the D P R.
Every week: the labour is paid, often in cash or by UPI, and next week's material is ordered.
And every month: the R A bill to the client, the subcontractor and supplier bills, a stock check, and the books go to the C A.

items: Books to the CA · GST · TDS

scenes.title: Money goes out every day. It comes in once a month, late.
beats: And here's the problem hidden in that rhythm.
Money goes out all the time: to suppliers, on thirty to sixty days' credit; to labour, every week; to subcontractors; and to salaries, fuel and hire.
But money comes in once a month, from the client, and usually late.
So the contractor pays for the client's building for one or two months, with its own money, supplier credit, or a bank overdraft.
On top of that, the client often holds back about five percent of every bill, as retention. It's real money owed, and it's easy to forget.
That's why every late or short bill hurts: it's one more week of financing someone else's building.

gap.text: The cash gap: 1–2 months funded by the contractor
gap.sub: own money · supplier credit · bank overdraft

retention.text: ~5% of every bill held as retention

scenes.title: The ten biggest money leaks
beats: So where does the profit actually disappear? Here are the ten biggest leaks.
Material paid for, but never received: short lorries, accepted on the delivery note.
Material used beyond the work: nine bags of cement, where the work needed seven.
Labour not matched by output: six thousand four hundred rupees of masons, for four thousand rupees of plastering.
Subcontractors overpaid. Bills to the client sent late, or short. Supplier bills paid twice, or at the wrong rate.
Idle time, when a team waits a whole day for cement that ran out. And rework, when a slab is broken and redone.
Petty cash with no bills. And retention and advances, simply forgotten.
None of these is dramatic on its own. Together, they're the difference between profit and loss.

footer.text: Small leaks. Together: profit or loss.

scenes.title: Everything is recorded somewhere. Nothing is known in time.
beats: Here's the strange part. The company usually already has all of this information.
It's in paper registers on site, which reach the office days later, if they ever do.
It's in WhatsApp chats and photos, where everything is there, and nothing can be found or added up.
It's in Excel files: one person's file, in many versions. It's in Tally: accurate, but after the fact. And it's in phone calls, answered from memory.
So problems are found at month end, at closeout, or by the accountant, when it's too late to do anything about them.
What the general manager we met asked for was the opposite: to know the same day, while it can still be fixed.

scenes.title: Follow 200 bags through the whole business
beats: Let's put it all together, and follow one load of cement through the whole business.
The BOQ has a hundred and twenty cubic metres of concrete. That needs about nine hundred and sixty bags of cement, budgeted at four hundred rupees a bag.
The site engineer sees the first-floor slab is due on Friday, with only thirty bags left. So they ask for two hundred.
Purchase orders two hundred bags from the supplier, at four hundred rupees a bag, plus GST.
On Tuesday the lorry arrives. Three bags are torn, and rejected. A hundred and ninety-seven are accepted.
On Friday the slab is poured: twenty-four cubic metres, using all two hundred bags. It should have taken about a hundred and ninety-two. That's four percent over.
Then the supplier's bill arrives: two hundred bags, at four hundred and twenty rupees. It matches neither the order, nor the delivery. Corrected, it's five thousand two hundred rupees less.
At month end, the slab is measured and billed to the client, minus five percent retention.
Without connected records, nobody would have seen that the cement was four percent over, the bill was five thousand two hundred rupees too high, and three bags never arrived.

footer.text: Three problems nobody sees, unless the records are connected.

scenes.title: One business, nine connected parts
beats: And that's the whole business on one map.
Planning sets what to build and what it should cost. Procurement buys it. Materials knows what's on site. The site records what happened each day.
Labour and subcontract knows who worked, and what they produced. Cost control compares every day's cost with the value of the work done.
Finance pays and keeps the books. Client billing turns measured work into money. And the owner's view sits on top of all of it.
Every part feeds the next. When they're connected, the owner knows the same day.
In episode two, we'll meet the owners themselves: what they're afraid of, what they want, and why they buy.
